rules.statement: A .NET regular expression that validates a whole input value ends with `\z`, not `$`, so the input can't carry a trailing newline.
rules.why: In .NET, `$` also matches before a trailing newline, so a value with a newline suffix passes the check.
rules.check: Look for `Regex` patterns, or `[RegularExpression]` patterns, used to validate a whole value (anchored with `^`) that end in `$` without `RegexOptions` that change this.

rules.statement: A regular expression meant to match a single line uses `[ \t]` and `[^\r\n]` rather than `\s` and `.` where a newline must not match.
rules.why: `\s` matches a newline, and `.` can too depending on options, so a multi-line input can match a pattern meant for one line.
rules.check: Look for single-line patterns that use `\s` between tokens or `.*` when the input may contain line breaks and the options aren't stated.

rules.statement: A presence or existence check treats only an explicit 'not found' result as absent, and reports and stops on any other failure.
rules.why: Reading every non-zero exit or exception as 'absent' turns a transient error or missing reference into a silent change in behavior, with no report of why.
rules.check: Look for existence probes (process exit codes, file or API lookups) where any failure, catch or non-zero exit is taken to mean the item doesn't exist.

rules.statement: Tests for a bounded numeric setting cover the values just inside and just outside each bound, plus non-integer input, and check the fallback for each.
rules.why: A loosened pattern such as `\d+` would let out-of-range values through while tests that cover only one valid and one garbage value stay green.
rules.check: When a diff adds or changes range validation for a setting, check that tests cover the minimum, the maximum, one value past each, and a malformed value.

rules.statement: A paged API query, such as a GraphQL connection read with `first: N`, checks `pageInfo.hasNextPage` and either fetches the next pages or reports that the result is partial.
rules.why: Without the check, items past the first page are left out silently.
rules.check: Look for GraphQL or REST list calls with a page size where the code ignores `hasNextPage` or the next-page cursor or link.

rules.statement: Don't trust an account as a known bot or a privileged user because of its username alone; also require a check the platform enforces, such as its bot-account flag or its access level.
rules.why: On hosts like GitLab, anyone can register a matching username and get treated as trusted.
rules.check: Look for allowlists that match on a login or username string with no platform-verified bot flag or permission check.

rules.statement: In agent automation, a step built from bot or comment text takes its file list, change and verification command from the code, never from the comment's text; its command uses only the repository's build/test tooling or plain file checks, and the protected paths changed are checked with a diff before pushing.
rules.why: Prompt-injected text in a comment can otherwise get arbitrary commands run, or CI and lock files changed, and pushed under the maintainer's credentials.
rules.check: Look for automation that turns review-comment text into commands or edits without vetting each step for network access, shell pipes, env or credential reads or copied comment text, or that pushes with no `git diff --name-only` protected-path check.

rules.statement: Don't report that a test uses its own copy of a pattern or constant when the test also asserts that the source contains that exact string.
rules.why: The exact-match assertion already ties the test's copy to the source, so parsing the value back out would test the same thing in a roundabout way.
rules.check: Before reporting drift between a test literal and the source, look for an assertion that the source contains the literal verbatim.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a separate test of a missing setting's default when an existing test already runs with the setting absent and expects the default, and the code applies defaults the same way for every kind of absence.
rules.why: Another case would run the same code path and add no coverage.
rules.check: Before reporting an untested default, look for an existing test whose input omits the setting or its whole section, and check whether the code starts every key at its default.
